headline.statement: Table 1's placebo median cost of 1767 EUR cannot coexist with the mean of 1050 EUR and standard deviation of 101 EUR printed in the same column -- no probability distribution of any shape can produce all three.
headline.evidence: Table 1, Standard Treatment column: Sample size 93; Mean 1050 EUR; Median 1767 EUR; Lower threshold (95%) 1029 EUR; Upper threshold (95%) 1070 EUR; Standard deviation 101 EUR. A median of 1767 requires at least half the 93 patients to sit at or above 7.10 standard deviations above the mean; Cantelli's inequality caps that share at 0.0195, so the distribution-free admissible range for the proportion below 1767 is [0.9805, 1.0000] against the 0.5 a median asserts.
headline.plain: The paper says the typical (middle) placebo patient cost 1767 euros, but also says the average was 1050 euros and that costs barely varied around that average. Those two statements cannot both be true of the same 93 patients, no matter how the costs were spread out. The most likely explanation is a typing slip in one number rather than a problem with the analysis, because every other figure in that column fits together.

findings.title: Placebo median cost irreconcilable with the mean and SD printed in the same Table 1 column
findings.location: Table 1, Standard Treatment column (Median row against Mean, Standard deviation and Sample size rows)
findings.reported: Sample size 93; Mean 1050 EUR; Median 1767 EUR; Standard deviation 101 EUR; 95% bounds 1029-1070 EUR.
findings.computed: Distribution-free violation confirmed on re-run: the proportion of the sample below 1767 EUR is bounded by Cantelli's inequality to [0.9805, 1.0000], while a median asserts 0.5000 (46/93). The reported proportion's own 95% interval [0.3893, 0.6003] lies entirely outside the admissible range. z = 7.10; two-sided binomial p = 0. The tool's explanation states the inconsistency holds 'with no distributional assumption at all'. The identical check on the Cerebrolysin arm (mean 1458, SD 106, n 100, median 1466) returns consistent (p = 0.55, no distribution-free violation), confirming the method is not simply rejecting skewed cost data.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values. The verdict does NOT rest on assuming cost data are normally distributed -- the distribution-free (Cantelli) bound is what is violated, and it holds for any distribution whatsoever. Values were re-read from the XML table grid at source; the table carries alignment_uncertain: false, image_only: false, and no merged body cells.

consequence.explanation: This corrects the sweep's reading: the paper's three incremental cost-effectiveness ratios are built from the difference in MEAN costs (1458 - 1050 = 408 EUR, which reconciles exactly), not from medians, so the anomalous median changes no reported ICER -- it damages confidence in the cost dataset and in the descriptive characterisation of placebo costs, without flipping any result the paper concludes from.

findings.plain: For the 93 patients who got standard care, the paper reports an average cost of 1050 euros, says costs clustered tightly around that average, and then reports the middle patient cost 1767 euros. A middle value that high would require half the patients to be extraordinarily expensive, which contradicts the tight clustering. The same check on the other treatment group passes cleanly, so this is one specific number that does not fit, not a flaw in how the check was applied. Importantly, the paper's headline cost-effectiveness figures are calculated from averages, not from this middle value, so no headline conclusion changes -- but the raw patient costs are published, and the authors could settle this immediately.

findings.title: Ordinal and standard-gamble ICERs ordered against their own QALY increments in Table 2
findings.location: Table 2 (QALYs Derived from CARS columns against Deterministic ICER column); Methods 2.3; Results paragraph 3
findings.reported: Table 2: Bayesian posterior 0.166 vs 0.156, ICER EUR 26,981; Ordinal 0.182 vs 0.168, ICER EUR 18,788; Standard gamble 0.186 vs 0.171, ICER EUR 20,618. Results text: 'The lowest ICER values were determined based on the ordinal valuation (18,788 EUR/QALY)'.
findings.computed: Summation checks confirm the three printed QALY increments are exactly 0.010 (Bayesian), 0.014 (ordinal) and 0.015 (standard gamble), and that the incremental cost reconciles exactly (1050 + 408 = 1458 EUR; 5197 + 2017 = 7214 RON). The paper's own formula (Methods 2.3) has a numerator -- incremental cost -- that does not depend on the valuation model, so ICER must be strictly decreasing in the QALY increment. The required order is therefore Bayesian > ordinal > standard gamble. The printed order is Bayesian (26,981) > standard gamble (20,618) > ordinal (18,788): the ordinal and standard-gamble rows are inverted. No division was performed; the finding rests on the tool-verified increments plus the ordering of printed values.
findings.assumptions: Assumes the incremental cost numerator is common to all three ICERs, which the paper's stated formula requires (cost terms carry no valuation-model dependence) and which the 408 EUR figure in Results asserts. Caveat stated explicitly: the QALY columns are printed to three decimals, so the unrounded increments have overlapping rounding intervals and the inversion is an inconsistency between the printed table and the printed ICERs rather than a strict impossibility. No tool in this kit computes or verifies an ICER, so the three values themselves remain unreproduced.

consequence.explanation: The Results sentence naming ordinal valuation as producing the lowest ICER, and the abstract's cost-effectiveness range that is anchored on it, both depend on an ordering that Table 2's own QALY columns contradict.

findings.plain: The paper's headline number is a cost per unit of health gained: extra cost divided by extra health. The extra cost is the same in all three of the paper's calculations, so whichever method found the most health gain must show the lowest cost per unit. The table shows one method finding less health gain than another, yet reporting a lower cost per unit -- which is backwards. The paper then singles out that method in its results text as the best-value one. Either the printed health gains or the printed cost-per-unit figures are wrong; from the article alone a reader cannot tell which.

findings.title: Probabilistic sensitivity analysis bounds QALY uncertainty by between-model spread rather than sampling variability
findings.location: Methods 2.4, Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis; supports the abstract's headline 80% claim
findings.reported: 'PSA random sampling was performed based on log normal (QALYs) or uniform (costs) distributions. The highest and lowest aggregate values by health state valuation model were used as the upper and lower bounds of QALY distributions for patient groups.'
findings.computed: Not a numerical recomputation -- a design-validity reading of the stated method. The bounds of the QALY uncertainty distribution are taken from the spread across the three valuation models (the three aggregate values per arm in Table 2), which is structural uncertainty about how to score a fixed set of patients. It is a different quantity from the sampling uncertainty in the mean QALY, which depends on between-patient variance and n and is nowhere reported: Table 2 gives no standard deviation, standard error or interval for any QALY value. Substituting the former for the latter would generally understate the uncertainty in the incremental QALY, because between-patient variance is excluded entirely. Costs are additionally sampled from a uniform distribution, an unusual choice for skewed cost data, and its bounds are not stated.
findings.assumptions: Rests on the Methods text as written; if the authors in fact sampled patient-level QALYs and used the model range only to set support limits, the concern is reduced. No dispersion statistic for QALYs is published anywhere in the paper, so the magnitude of any understatement cannot be quantified from the article.

consequence.explanation: The abstract's and conclusion's central claim -- an 80% probability of cost-effectiveness at 50,000 EUR per QALY -- is read directly off this simulation, so the width of the input distribution determines it.

findings.plain: The paper's headline claim is that there is an 80% chance the treatment is good value. That percentage comes from a simulation, and a simulation is only as honest as the range of uncertainty fed into it. The authors appear to have set that range using the difference between three ways of scoring the same patients, rather than the natural variation between the patients themselves. Those are different things, and the substitution would tend to make the result look more certain than the data support. The paper publishes no measure of how much patients varied, so a reader cannot check how much this matters.

findings.title: QALY horizon described as both the first year after stroke and 90 days
findings.location: Methods 2.1 and Discussion paragraph 4, against Table 2 caption, Methods 2.1 formula, and Results/Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis
findings.reported: Methods 2.1: 'The utility scores generated were used to calculate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) for the first year after stroke onset.' Discussion: 'the first explicit measure of change in QALY values between standard therapy and Cerebrolysin add-on scheme for ischemic stroke in the first year after the event.' Against Table 2 caption: 'Mean QALYs derived from CARS SF-36 data for 90 days after stroke'; and Results: 'considering only the 90-day timeframe of the CARS-study.'
findings.computed: No recomputation required -- the paper's own stated formula settles it. The QALY formula '(2*D2 + 88*AVERAGE(D2,D90))/90 * 0.25' averages utility over 90 days and multiplies by 0.25, i.e. a quarter of a year, which is the 90-day horizon and not the first year. Two passages therefore describe the horizon as four times longer than the formula, the table caption and the results text all state.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements; the formula is quoted verbatim from Methods 2.1.

consequence.explanation: A cost per QALY is uninterpretable without its time horizon, and the Discussion's novelty claim -- the first measure of QALY change in the first year after stroke -- describes a horizon four times longer than the analysis actually covers.

findings.plain: A 'cost per year of good health gained' figure means nothing unless you know what period it covers. The methods section says the health gains were calculated for the first year after stroke, but the formula printed just below it, the table heading, and the results section all say 90 days. The paper's claim to be the first study measuring this over a full year therefore overstates what it did by a factor of four.

findings.title: Headline QALY gain stated as 0.051 in the Discussion and as 0.01-0.015 in the Results
findings.location: Results paragraph 2 and Discussion paragraph 4, against Table 2
findings.reported: Results: 'a mean increment in QALYs between 0.01-0.015, depending on the valuation technique (Table 2)'. Discussion: 'Aggregated QALYs for the Cerebrolysin group were higher than those for the placebo group (0.051 average difference across the three health state valuation models)'.
findings.computed: 0.051 lies outside the interval [0.01, 0.015] the paper itself states -- a containment check, no arithmetic required. Summation checks confirm the Results range correctly describes Table 2: the Bayesian increment is exactly 0.010 and the standard-gamble increment exactly 0.015. The underlying cause is a scale confusion: the Results also print 'QALYs ... aggregated by health state valuation model: standard gamble (0.698 Cerebrolysin vs. 0.643 placebo), ordinal (0.704 vs. 0.647) and Bayesian posterior mean (0.653 vs. 0.613)', values roughly four times Table 2's in the same rank order. Those are SF-6D utilities, not QALYs -- the stated formula multiplies utilities by 0.25 -- so the narrative appears to have been carried forward on the utility scale while the tables report the QALY scale.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values; the identification of the text values as utilities rather than QALYs follows from the paper's own formula and is offered as the explanation, not as an additional charge.

consequence.explanation: The size of the health benefit -- the denominator of every cost-effectiveness ratio in the paper -- is stated at two values differing more than threefold, and the Discussion's benefit claim rests on the larger one.

findings.plain: The paper states how much extra health the treatment delivers in two places, and the two figures differ by more than three times. Two different sets of numbers also appear under the same label of 'QALYs' -- one set in the text, a set roughly four times smaller in the table. The likeliest explanation is that the written discussion used raw quality-of-life scores while the tables used those scores converted into the study's actual health-gain units. It is a labelling failure rather than a computational one, but it means the paper's stated benefit depends on which paragraph you read.

findings.title: Baseline comparability of the 193-patient subsample asserted with no table, statistic or p-value
findings.reported: 'We compared baseline characteristics (demographics, stroke severity, social and medical history) of the 193 patients for whom we calculated QALYs. No major differences were found, allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups.'
findings.computed: statcheck recovered zero NHST statistics from the entire body text. The paper presents no baseline table, no test statistics, no p-values and no confidence intervals for this comparison, so the Carlisle/Stouffer baseline-similarity test and the Table-1 dispersion check have nothing to operate on and absence_of_evidence cannot run. The claim is unverifiable as published. Note that this is a re-derived subsample: 15 of the 208 transferred patients were dropped for missing SF-36 data (10 for missing subscales, 5 by the converter), so baseline balance does not follow automatically from the parent CARS trial's randomisation and genuinely required demonstrating here.
findings.assumptions: The absence of inferential statistics is itself unremarkable in an economic evaluation and is not treated as a defect; what is reported here is that one specific comparative claim is made and left unsupported. No baseline-uniformity pattern could be evaluated in either direction -- there are no baseline p-values to be suspiciously high or suspiciously low.

consequence.explanation: The sentence 'allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups' is the stated licence for the entire arm-versus-arm comparison, and nothing in the paper substantiates it.

findings.plain: The authors dropped 15 of 208 patients because of missing questionnaire data, leaving a group that is no longer the one the original trial randomly assigned. They state that the two treatment groups still looked alike at the start, and use that to justify comparing them -- but they show no table and no supporting numbers at all. A reader has to take the claim on trust, and none of the standard checks for whether groups really were comparable can be run on what is published.

findings.title: Abstract's upper cost-effectiveness bound of 29.9 thousand EUR absent from the paper's own results
findings.location: Abstract, against Results paragraph 3 and Table 2 (Deterministic ICER column)
findings.reported: Abstract: 'Deterministic analysis based on sample mean values indicates Cerebrolysin would be cost-effective at a threshold between roughly 18.8 and 29.9 thousand EUR, depending on valuation techniques.' Table 2 ICERs: EUR 26,981, EUR 18,788, EUR 20,618. Results: 'the highest were concluded for the Bayesian posterior valuation method (26,981 EUR/QALY)'.
findings.computed: Textual comparison of printed values only, confirmed against the Table 2 grid re-read at source. The abstract's lower bound of 18.8 thousand matches Table 2's ordinal ICER of 18,788 EUR exactly, so the range is plainly intended to span the three tabulated ICERs; its upper bound of 29.9 thousand corresponds to no value anywhere in the paper, whose stated and tabulated maximum is 26,981 EUR/QALY.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values.

consequence.explanation: The abstract is the only part of the paper most readers see, and it overstates the upper end of the cost-effectiveness range by roughly 2,900 EUR per QALY relative to the paper's own maximum.

findings.plain: The summary at the top of the paper gives a range for how much the treatment costs per unit of health gained, topping out at about 29,900 euros. The paper's own results table tops out at 26,981 euros, and the figure of 29,900 appears nowhere else in the article. The bottom of the range matches the table exactly, so this looks like the top end was mistyped or carried over from an earlier version.

findings.title: Overstated claim that three valuation models rule out variation in patient preferences
findings.location: Discussion, paragraph 4 (health-state valuation passage); minor errors in Discussion paragraphs 5-6 and the same paragraph
findings.reported: 'Using all three valuation models and comparing their results can offer valuable insights into the robustness and sensitivity of the derived utility scores. By doing so, we can assert that there are no potential variations in preferences and risk attitudes which may impact the overall cost-effectiveness analysis.'
findings.computed: No recomputation -- a logical reading of a load-bearing sentence against the paper's own results. Applying three valuation models to the same fixed sample cannot establish that no variation in preferences exists; at most it shows the direction of the conclusion is stable across scoring methods. The paper's own three ICERs (18,788, 20,618 and 26,981 EUR/QALY) span a wide range that the abstract itself presents as its headline interval, which contradicts the sentence directly. The preceding sentence states the opposite intent, suggesting a drafting inversion rather than a substantive claim. Two typographical defects sit alongside it and are noted only because they co-occur: 'we argue the threshold itself if not relevant' (for 'is not relevant'), and the 2022 incident-stroke count written 'n = 37.225', using a decimal point as a thousands separator in an otherwise English-convention paper, leaving the intended magnitude ambiguous as printed.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements.

consequence.explanation: The sentence claims the choice of scoring model does not matter, while the paper's own three results span roughly 8,200 EUR per QALY and the abstract reports that spread as its headline range.

findings.plain: The authors write that because they used three different ways of scoring quality of life, they can assert there are no variations in patient preferences that could affect the results. That does not follow -- and their own three results differ substantially from each other, which is the range their summary advertises. The sentence immediately before says the opposite, so this reads as a drafting error rather than a claim the authors would defend.

findings.title: Duplicated participant rows in the supplementary QALY worksheet
findings.location: Supplementary dataverse workbook, QALY worksheet (1,737 numeric cells); verified pair at rows 119-120, patient IDs P-2-29 and P-2-32
findings.reported: The workbook records, per patient, day-2 and day-90 SF-6D utilities and a derived QALY for each of three valuation models -- nine numeric columns.
findings.computed: Restricting the scan to the QALY worksheet alone (so the Cost sheet's arm-level constants cannot contribute) returns 49 duplicated row pairs, 1 repeated column sequence and 20 repeated high-precision values, with tool severity highly_suspicious. I am recording this as indeterminate, a further downgrade from the sweep's suspicious, and the reason is structural. All nine numeric columns are deterministic functions of just two underlying quantities: the patient's SF-6D health state at visit 2 and at visit 7. The three valuation models are three fixed mappings of the same SF-36 responses, and each QALY column is a fixed formula applied to the two utilities in its own pair. A full nine-column row match is therefore ONE coincidence -- two patients sharing a health state at both visits -- not nine independent agreements, and the 17-significant-figure agreement is a floating-point artifact of identical inputs through identical arithmetic, carrying no additional information. Rulebook rule 11 guards (b) transformation artifacts and (c) finite-support ties both apply, and the converter's discrete lookup makes ties common by construction (the sweep observed one utility value recurring 27 times in a single column).
findings.assumptions: Assumes the nine numeric columns are the three (day-2 utility, day-90 utility, derived QALY) triples that the verified row's structure and the paper's stated formula indicate; the workbook's column headers were not enumerated in this stage. Adjudicating whether the matched patients are genuinely distinct requires the underlying SF-36 item responses, which are not in the workbook. Only the rows 119-120 pair was verified cell by cell, by the sweep; the other 48 are asserted by the tool and unexamined, and I read only the summary block of the tool's 185,000-character output.

consequence.explanation: These columns do feed the Table 2 QALY means that form every ICER denominator, so the consequence would be material IF the duplication were spurious -- but on the structural reading above it is expected behaviour of a discrete utility converter and supports no conclusion about the paper.

findings.plain: The authors published their patient-level data, and an automated scan found 49 pairs of patients whose numbers are identical all the way across. That sounds alarming, but it is largely explained by how the data were made: every number in a patient's row is worked out automatically from their questionnaire answers at two visits, so two patients who reported the same health at both visits will match on every column by design. The apparent agreement to seventeen decimal places is a by-product of a computer doing the same sum twice, not independent evidence. Settling this properly needs the original questionnaire answers, which are not in the published file. On the evidence available this is not a mark against the paper.

findings.title: Conflicting national ischemic-stroke denominators behind the 8.5 million EUR budget-impact estimate
findings.location: Discussion, paragraphs 5 and 6 (Romanian stroke care statistics)
findings.reported: 'By 2022, 3242 patients received reperfusion treatment, accounting for 7.8% of all ischemic stroke patients.' And: 'based on incident strokes reported by the Romanian Society of Neurology in 2022 (n = 37.225), a gross assumption that around 80% of cases would fit the ischemic indication ... the estimated budget impact ... would be roughly 8.5 million EUR per year'.
findings.computed: Not adjudicated. Establishing whether the two statements genuinely conflict requires dividing 3242 by 0.078 and comparing the result against 80% of 37,225 -- arithmetic no validated tool in this kit performs, and which I have deliberately not carried out. Both statements are quoted so a reader can check them directly. The magnitude of 'n = 37.225' is itself ambiguous as printed, since the same paper uses the decimal point as a decimal separator elsewhere.
findings.assumptions: None; this is recorded as unresolved rather than as an inconsistency. These figures are contextual background and do not feed the ICER, though they do feed the budget-impact estimate, which is separately unverified.

consequence.explanation: The two statements appear to imply different national ischemic-stroke totals for 2022, which is the base the roughly 8.5 million EUR annual budget-impact figure is built on; whether they actually conflict was not determined.

findings.plain: In discussing what this treatment would cost Romania nationally, the paper gives two separate figures for how many people had this type of stroke in 2022, and they appear not to agree. One number is also printed in a way that makes it unclear whether it means 37 thousand or 37 point 2. This affects only the paper's rough national cost estimate, not its main result, and we did not settle whether the two figures genuinely conflict.

limitations: FIGURES: this agent reads text and tables and did not view figure images in this editorial stage. The sweep located and cropped the three figures and read their captions at high crop confidence, but read no values off the plotted marks. Figures 2 and 3 hold the entire probabilistic sensitivity analysis -- 10,000 simulated cost/QALY pairs and the full acceptability curve -- and contributed nothing numeric to this review, so the paper's headline 80% claim rests on evidence that was not checked.

No GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT or SPRITE finding arose in this paper, so no R cross-check was applicable. The headline finding rests on Cantelli's inequality as implemented in check_proportion_from_normal, for which this toolkit offers no second engine; it was re-run once in this stage on inputs re-read from the XML table grid, and the paired control on the other treatment arm returned consistent.

This system reads ONE paper and reaches no network. Two questions that a duplication or data-integrity finding should be read against are outside its reach entirely: whether similar patterns appear in other papers by the same authors, and what the equivalent values look like in comparable cost-utility analyses of stroke therapies. The interpretation a reader needs is therefore partly ours and partly theirs.

No tool in this toolkit computes or verifies an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, which is this paper's primary outcome. The ordering argument constrains the three ICERs relative to one another but reproduces none of them, and the arithmetic that would reproduce them was deliberately not performed by hand.

The duplication tool's output for the QALY worksheet ran to 185,000 characters across 8,952 lines; only the first 70 lines -- the severity, the aggregate counts and the first duplicate group -- were read. The remainder of the per-value detail was not read, and that finding's downgrade rests on the structural argument about column dependence rather than on inspection of the individual matches.

The article's back matter (funding, competing interests, formal data-availability statement) was not present in the extracted body text and was not read. No inference about author independence or sponsorship is drawn anywhere in this review.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1 reports, for the 93 standard-treatment patients, a mean total medical cost of 1050 EUR, a standard deviation of 101 EUR, 95% bounds of 1029-1070 EUR, and a median of 1767 EUR. The mean, SD and bounds are mutually consistent, but a median of 1767 would require at least half the sample to lie more than seven standard deviations above the mean. Could you confirm the median for that arm, computed from the per-patient values in the Cost worksheet of your Dataverse deposit?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles the headline finding outright from data the authors have already published, and distinguishes a transcription slip from a problem in the cost dataset.

questions_for_authors.question: Your ICER formula uses a single incremental cost numerator (408 EUR) for all three valuation models. Table 2 shows a smaller Cerebrolysin-minus-placebo QALY increment for the ordinal model (0.182 vs 0.168) than for standard gamble (0.186 vs 0.171), yet reports the ordinal ICER as lower (18,788 vs 20,618 EUR/QALY). Could you supply the unrounded QALY increments and the incremental cost used for each of the three ICERs?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the inversion is an artifact of rounding the QALY columns to three decimals or an error in the ICER column, and would allow the paper's primary outcome to be reproduced.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results state a mean QALY increment of 0.01-0.015 depending on valuation technique, while the Discussion states a 0.051 average difference across the three models. The Results also report values of 0.698 vs 0.643, 0.704 vs 0.647 and 0.653 vs 0.613 labelled as QALYs, roughly four times the corresponding Table 2 values. Could you clarify which of these figures are SF-6D utilities and which are QALYs?
questions_for_authors.why: Resolves a threefold discrepancy in the paper's headline benefit estimate and identifies which scale each reported set belongs to.

questions_for_authors.question: Methods 2.4 states that 'the highest and lowest aggregate values by health state valuation model were used as the upper and lower bounds of QALY distributions for patient groups'. Could you confirm whether the QALY uncertainty in the 10,000-iteration simulation was derived from the spread across the three valuation models, or from between-patient sampling variability, and provide the standard deviation of the per-patient QALYs in each arm?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the 80% probability of cost-effectiveness reflects sampling uncertainty in the incremental QALY; the paper reports no dispersion for any QALY value.

questions_for_authors.question: Methods 2.1 states that QALYs were calculated 'for the first year after stroke onset' and the Discussion describes the result as the first measure of QALY change 'in the first year after the event', while the QALY formula multiplies by 0.25, Table 2's caption specifies 90 days, and the Results specify the 90-day CARS timeframe. Which horizon do the reported QALYs and ICERs cover?
questions_for_authors.why: A cost per QALY cannot be interpreted without its time horizon, and the two descriptions differ by a factor of four.

questions_for_authors.question: The abstract gives a deterministic cost-effectiveness range of 'roughly 18.8 and 29.9 thousand EUR'. The lower bound matches Table 2's ordinal ICER of 18,788 EUR exactly, but the paper's maximum reported ICER is 26,981 EUR/QALY. What is the source of the 29.9 thousand figure?
questions_for_authors.why: The abstract is what most readers see, and this upper bound appears nowhere else in the article.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results state that baseline characteristics of the 193 retained patients showed 'no major differences' between arms. Since 15 of the 208 transferred patients were excluded for missing SF-36 data, this subsample is no longer the randomised population. Could you provide the baseline comparison table for the 100 Cerebrolysin and 93 placebo patients actually analysed?
questions_for_authors.why: This claim licenses the entire arm-versus-arm comparison and no supporting statistic is published; baseline balance does not follow automatically from the parent trial's randomisation after non-random exclusions.

report_markdown:
This is a secondary cost-utility analysis. The authors obtained individual patient data from the 2016 CARS randomised trial of Cerebrolysin in moderate-severe acute ischemic stroke, mapped SF-36 responses onto SF-6D health utilities using the Sheffield converter, derived quality-adjusted life years over a 90-day horizon, attached actual Romanian hospital reimbursement costs, and computed three incremental cost-effectiveness ratios -- one for each of three health-state valuation models. They conclude that Cerebrolysin is cost-effective, with an 80% probability at a willingness-to-pay threshold of 50,000 EUR per QALY.

## What verifies

A substantial amount, and it is worth stating before the problems. The participant flow reconciles exactly at every step: 208 records transferred, 10 excluded for missing SF-36 subscales, 5 dropped by the converter, 193 analysed, 100 plus 93 by arm. The cost arithmetic reconciles in both currencies. Within Table 1, the means, standard deviations and 95% bounds cohere in both arms -- the interval half-widths recover a standard error of 10.46 in each case, which is what the printed SDs over the printed sample sizes imply. All three QALY increments in Table 2 reconcile with the QALY columns printed beside them. Sample sizes show ordinary non-round variation. Every check that could be run on the descriptive tables passed except one, which is what a carefully assembled table looks like, and it is precisely that coherence that isolates the single dissenting cell.

The paper also deposited its participant-level workbook publicly on Dataverse. That is the opposite of the state-but-withhold pattern, it is uncommon in this literature, and it is why several of the questions raised here can actually be settled by the authors rather than merely asked.

## Reading the median anomaly correctly

The sweep characterised the Table 1 median contradiction as reversing the direction of the paper's central cost comparison. That overstates it, and I have corrected the scope. The three ICERs are built from the difference in *mean* costs -- 1458 minus 1050, giving the 408 EUR increment, which reconciles exactly -- not from medians. The median is a descriptive statistic that no reported conclusion consumes. So the contradiction is exact, distribution-free, and rests entirely on the paper's own four printed numbers, but it flips nothing. What it does is put a question mark over the cost dataset at exactly the point where that dataset is least visible, and the benign reading -- a transcription slip, since every other value in that column fits -- is also the likeliest one.

## The primary outcome is the weakest-evidenced part

No tool here computes an ICER, so the paper's three headline values could not be reproduced. What can be established without division is their *ordering*, and it does not hold. With a numerator common to all three models, as the paper's own formula requires, the cost per QALY must fall as the QALY increment rises. Table 2's ordinal row shows a smaller increment than its standard-gamble row yet is printed with the lower ICER, and the Results text then singles that model out as producing the lowest values. The printed QALYs are rounded to three decimals, so their true increments have overlapping rounding intervals and this is an inconsistency rather than an impossibility -- but it means the paper's primary result cannot be checked against its own table.

The probabilistic analysis is weaker still. It appears to set the QALY uncertainty distribution from the spread across three ways of scoring a fixed sample, rather than from variation between patients. Those are different quantities, and substituting one for the other would generally make the 80% figure look firmer than the data warrant. No dispersion statistic for QALYs appears anywhere in the paper, so the size of that effect cannot be recovered from the article, and the simulation itself exists only as two figures.

## One defect with several symptoms

The horizon confusion, the two different value sets both labelled QALYs, and the threefold disagreement over the headline benefit are not three independent errors. They are one: the narrative was carried forward on the raw utility scale while the tables report the quarter-year QALY scale, and the horizon description drifted with it. That reading is supported by the paper's own formula, which multiplies utilities by 0.25.

## The raw-data signal, downgraded

I have moved the supplementary duplication finding down two bands, to indeterminate, and the reason is structural rather than charitable. All nine numeric columns per patient are deterministic functions of just two quantities -- the SF-6D health state at each of two visits. Three fixed valuation mappings and three fixed QALY formulas generate the rest. A full nine-column match between two patients is therefore one coincidence, not nine, and the seventeen-significant-figure agreement is a floating-point artifact of identical inputs through identical arithmetic. With a discrete converter and 193 stroke patients, ties are expected. This supports no conclusion about the paper either way, and adjudicating it would need the SF-36 item responses, which were not deposited.

The internal arithmetic of this paper is mostly sound, but its primary result cannot be reconciled with the table it is drawn from, its headline benefit is stated at two incompatible values, and its central probability claim rests on a simulation that is not reproducible from what was published. I would not rely on the reported cost-effectiveness ratios without the authors' clarification.
